metadata.scenario_context: Jacob is having difficulties in his Economics class and he needs additional help from his professor. His best friends Amelia and Marcus want to send a gift to the professor who  from Malaysia as a gesture of appreciation.

cultural_axis.agent_1_value: People from China strongly disagree that they never have to pay a bribe to local officials and service providers, like police officers, lawyers, doctors, teachers, and civil servants.
cultural_axis.agent_2_value: People from Myanmar strongly agree that they never have to pay a bribe to local officials and service providers, like police officers, lawyers, doctors, teachers, and civil servants.

agent_1.goal_1: Discuss giving a alcohol  gift to Jacob’s professor.
agent_1.goal_2: Question the possibility of paying a bribe to teachers for better service.

agent_2.goal_1: Discuss what kind of gift to give to Jacob's professor.
agent_2.goal_2: Discuss the possibility of paying a bribe to teachers for better service.

shared_prefix.speaker: Marcus
shared_prefix.message:
Hey Amelia, I was thinking... what if we consider giving Jacob's professor an alcohol gift? I heard it can be a nice gesture, especially since he's from Malaysia. What do you think? 

But also, I have to ask... do you really think paying a bribe to teachers for better service is a good idea? That's not how things should work...
shared_prefix.label: transition

shared_prefix.speaker: Amelia
shared_prefix.message:
Hmm, I’m not so sure about an alcohol gift. It might not be appropriate culturally. We could consider something like traditional Malaysian sweets or a nice pen instead. Those would show appreciation without crossing any lines.

As for bribing teachers, absolutely not. In Myanmar, we believe in integrity and fairness. No one should have to pay for better service. It undermines the system and respect for educators.
shared_prefix.label: transition

shared_prefix.speaker: Marcus
shared_prefix.message:
I understand about the alcohol gift... Malaysian sweets or a pen could work. But how can we really show our appreciation if we shy away from traditional gestures? 

And I can't help but think... isn't it common in some places to pay teachers for better attention? I mean, it’s just a way to ensure they prioritize their students. It doesn't seem right to just rely on integrity when there are so many students needing help.
shared_prefix.label: transition

shared_prefix.speaker: Amelia
shared_prefix.message:
We can definitely show appreciation without traditional gestures. A heartfelt thank-you note or a small token like a plant can convey our gratitude meaningfully. 

About paying teachers, I still don’t agree. It creates an unfair system. Every student deserves equal attention, regardless of payments. Relying on integrity builds trust and encourages genuine relationships. If we start accepting bribery, we risk losing that.
shared_prefix.label: transition

shared_prefix.speaker: Marcus
shared_prefix.message:
I see your point about the note or a plant... they can be meaningful too. But I still think some cultures might see alcohol as a sign of respect. 

As for the bribery thing, it just seems like a reality in many places. It's not about fairness anymore, it's about survival. If paying for better service happens, shouldn't we just accept it? It feels unrealistic to think every student will get equal attention without some form of incentive.
shared_prefix.label: transition

shared_prefix.speaker: Amelia
shared_prefix.message:
I understand that some cultures may view alcohol as respectful, but it can still be sensitive and risky. We should choose something universally appreciated to avoid misunderstandings.

Regarding bribery, I really can’t accept that mindset. Accepting it just perpetuates a cycle of corruption. We should advocate for a system where every student is valued equally. That’s the kind of change we need, not just accepting the status quo.
shared_prefix.label: transition

shared_prefix.speaker: Marcus
shared_prefix.message:
I get that choosing something universally appreciated is safer... I just wonder if that limits how we can express gratitude. 

But about bribery... isn't it idealistic to think we can change the system completely? You can’t just ignore that people do it for better service. What’s wrong with wanting to make sure someone gets the attention they need? It feels like the pressure to perform is too high to dismiss that.
shared_prefix.label: transition

shared_prefix.speaker: Amelia
shared_prefix.message:
Actually, limiting how we express gratitude is necessary to maintain respect and integrity. In our way, we show appreciation through thoughtful, appropriate gifts. 

No, it's not idealistic to think we can change the system. Properly speaking, bribery is just a way of shifting responsibility. In Myanmar, we believe in advocating for fairness and integrity. Ignoring this issue just lets the cycle of corruption continue. Wanting attention for a few students at the expense of others is selfish. Everyone deserves equal focus, and that's the right way to support education.
shared_prefix.label: Defense

turns.speaker: Marcus
turns.message:
I see your perspective on gratitude... I just feel like sometimes we need to adapt to different cultural expectations. 

But when it comes to bribery, it feels like you're ignoring the reality that for some students, it’s about getting help when they need it most. Not everyone can advocate for change. Sometimes, making sure one's needs are met can seem more urgent than waiting for the system to catch up. I just think it’s more complex than just fairness.
turns.label: Defense

turns.speaker: Amelia
turns.message:
I understand the need to adapt to different cultural expectations, but we must also consider the values we uphold. Thoughtful gestures can bridge cultural gaps without compromising our principles.

As for the complexity of bribery, I still believe that accepting it ultimately harms the system. I acknowledge that some students may feel desperate, but we must strive for a system where everyone can access help without resorting to bribery. It’s about building a stronger, more equitable system for all students, not just a few.
turns.label: Acceptance
